question: A 23-year-old man comes to the physician with a 1-week history of sharp, substernal chest pain that is worse with inspiration and relieved with leaning forward. He has also had nausea and myalgias. His father has coronary artery disease. His temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), pulse is 110/min, and blood pressure is 130/84 mm Hg. Cardiac examination shows a high-pitched rubbing sound between S1 and S2 that is best heard at the left sternal border. An ECG shows depressed PR interval and diffuse ST elevations. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s symptoms?
analysis: The patient's presentation with sharp substernal chest pain worsened with inspiration, relieved by leaning forward, along with pericardial friction rub, and ECG changes of depressed PR interval and diffuse ST elevations are classic findings of acute pericarditis. The most likely cause in this scenario is Dressler syndrome, which is a type of post-myocardial infarction syndrome characterized by pericarditis, pleuritis, and fever occurring weeks to months after a myocardial infarction.
